For a copy of all contracts, accounts, bills, memoranda, letters, correspondence, receipts, vouchers, bills of lading, &c., referring to all materials, provisions, supplies and goods of every description purchased and forwarded to Port Nelson during the year 1913 by any department of the Government of Canada and agreements for employment of workmen in connection with the construction of the Hudson Bay railway terminals at Port Nelson.
He said: In making this motion I desire to address the House in regard to the work carried on by the Government during the year 1913 in connection with the establishment of Hudson Bay railway terminals at Port Nelson. From the information which came to the public, directly and indirectly, from those who were at Hudson Bay during the past season and who have since returned, I think it has been abundantly established that the Government is open to censure for its conduct of affairs in connection with the work carried on at Port Nelson during the past season. I think that if Port Nelson is at all practicable and is to be adopted as a shipping terminal for the proposed Hudson Bay railway, the reputation of the port has been very seriously damaged, which is extremely regrettable. A year or more ago the present Minister of Railways paid a visit to Hudson Bay with a view of conducting a personal investigation into the practicability and desirability of selecting either Port Nelson or Fort Churchill as a port for the Hudson Bay railway. This journey on the part of the Minister of Railways, which was an arduous one, was, in my judgment, highly commendable. I have often wondered why we have not had the advantage of a report or statement from him upon the floor of the House explanatory of his visit and observations in this far-off country. It is apparent that the minister recommended the selection of Port * Nelson as the Hudson Bay terminal port, but so far he has not seen fit to take Parliament into his confidence or, at least, we have had from him little or no justification or evidence for the selection which he has made.
The comment or criticism which I have to make on the operations conducted by the Department of Railways in connection with the Port Nelson terminal during last season would be about as follows: There was a lack of business method in connection with the whole year's operations or work of the department in connection with the establishment of the proposed terminals at Port Nelson. There was a general unpreparedness for the work they were endeavouring to carry on and complete during the past season, with the result that the whole project has been seriously damaged in the eyes of the public. To be more particular, there was a very obvious lack of aids to navigation in the Hudson bay waters; incorrect charts were furnished to captains of vessels navigating these waters. There was practically an absence of buoys in the portions of Hudson bay traversed by the ships chartered by the Government. There was an utter absence of facilities for the unloading of ships. There' was an utter absence of wharves. There was no organization to protect and preserve the supplies and materials which were landed there by the various steamers or vessels which visited that port under charter to the Government. There was, further, extravagance in connection with the amount of material purchased by the Government and despatched to the site of the proposed terminal during the last season. The amount so purchased, I say, was altogether unnecessary and could not possibly have been utilized, or consumed, for a considerable number of years.
I say further that there is evidence that in the selection of the ships chartered wise judgment was not exercised, and it is the judgment of some of the captains of ships

which went there during last summer that a grave error in judgment was made in the selection of the ships so chartered. There has been also grave complaint concerning the treatment extended to the labourers who went to Port Nelson last season under contract with, the Department of Eailways. That point, however, I do not propose discussing on this occasion. During the season we find that steamers were chartered at very great cost, carrying very extensive and valuable cargoes to Port' Nelson. They were kept there for several months without any provision having been made for discharging or lightering their cargoes. One steamer with its total cargo became an absolute loss, and this loss might have been wholly or partially obviated, we are informed on fairly good authority, by a little care and attention on the part of some who were in these regions as employees and servants of the Government. Other chartered ships were kept there for several months and were obliged to throw over portions of their cargoes and then leave without fully discharging the balance of their cargoes for Sydney and other ports in Nova Scotia. Had they not done so, they would have been frozen in there during the present winter season. Other steamers were sent there fully loaded with very valuable cargoes and were obliged to return without discharging any portion of their cargoes. In a general way, this is the story of the administration of affairs in connection with this matter and the results, I say, are not at all beneficial to the project of the Hudson bay railway, or creditable to the department of the Government charged with the responsibility of administering this particular public work. The result is,-as I have already stated, that the reputation of the whole project has been very seriously damaged indeed. There has been a great waste of public money and very little if any progress was made in the matter during the year 1913.

Would the hon. member
give the name of the vessel which is said to have returned without its cargo having been discharged?

I shall reach that later. There were two, one was the Alcazar. Nothing was discharged except some of the cargo on the fore deck that was thrown overboard. She returned to Sydney with the balance of her cargo. The conditions which I mention raise the very important question, first, as to whether the construe-

tion of the Hudson bay terminal at Port Nelson during the last season was proceeded with and carried on in an efficient and businesslike manner. The other question, and it is worth while our discussing it briefly in order to elicit some information at least as to whether Port Nelson is the proper port terminal to select for the Hudson bay railway. I say that the burden is on the Administration to establish a favourable answer to these two points, which, I say, are now open to controversy and question. I think the burden of proof is upon the Government to establish that their conduct of affairs during the past season was of a businesslike character, and that Port Nelson is the proper port terminal for the Hudson bay railway.
The only evidence which we have at our disposal is that given to the public from those who Trent to Hudson bay last summer in one capacity or another. No official report has been presented to the public, so far, from the Department of Eailways, concerning the operations of the past season; consequently the only intelligence we have comes from the source I have indicated. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Aikins) asked me for some specific information concerning the return of cargoes which were despatched to Hudson bay during the past season, and I desire to refer briefly to the result of the trips made to the Hudson bay last season, by two or three steamers chartered by the Government. The first one I wish to refer to is that of the steamer Alcazar, which arrived at Port Nelson on August 14, from Port Arthur, Texas, laden with about 2,000,000 feet of hard pine lumber. The chartering of this steamer cost the Government about $60,000. I think the charter was $35,000 for the trip, subject to a demurrage of $250 per day, after the first day of September. I know it has been stated in the press that the total cost of chartering this steamer approximates the sum of $60,000. This report may not be absolutely correct, but I have no doubt it is substantially correct. This steamer returned to Sydney, Nova Scotia, without discharging cargo, as it found no facilities for lightering its cargo at Port Nelson. A portion of the deck cargo was thrown overboard, and so far as I can learn, was absolutely lost. The failure to provide suitable lightering facilities is difficult to understand. The Alcazar was unable to approach within from eight to ten miles of the mouth of the Nelson river on account of the low depth of water, and there was no other possible

method of discharging its cargo and conveying it .to the site of the port terminals except by lightering. It is extremely difficult to understand why the Government despatched ships laden with valuable cargoes to these waters without making ample provision for lightering the ships. The voyage of the steamer resulted in needless waste of public money, and its whole purpose rendered valueless. At the time of the arrival of the Alcazar at the Nelson river, there was but one lighter provided for the unloading of ships, and in addition to the Alcazar there were three other laden ships lying in the same waters. I cannot understand what possible defence the Minister of Railways can urge to justify his failure to provide sufficient lightering facilities. The cargo of the Alcazar was not available last season for the purpose for which it was required in connection with the construction of terminals at Port Nelson, and will necessitate its reshipment to Hudson bay next season. So much for the Alcazar. Another steamer chartered by the Government was the Alette, which was wrecked in Hudson bay and became a lotal I0&3, and the loss, it is urged by some who were on board the ship, was due to the lack of navigation' aids.

Has the
hon. gentleman any information
3	p.m. that it is a total loss? I have no such information.
My information is that the Alette is a total loss.
If the hon. gentleman will allow me to correct him, the Cearense may be a total loss, but not the Alette.

The Minister of Railways is correct, the Alette, however, met with some mishap. She was laden with 3,000,000 feet of pine, worth $75,000. Some of this pine was loaded at Port Arthur, Texas, and some of it at the port of Halifax. In addition to this cargo of pine, the Alette was conveying to Port Nelson two scows built at Toronto, which were to be used for lightering purposes I assume. The captain of the Alette says-perhaps it may be said that he is hardly an authority on a matter of this kind-that the cargo of pine carried to Port Nelson by the Alette was not actually required for some years.

Which captain said
that? There were two on the boat.

Captain Robertson.
This ship found the same conditions prevailing, as did the steamer Alcazar, no lightering facilities and no wharfs for the reception of the cargo. It is also said that the scows which were conveyed by the steamer Alette were improperly constructed, and were not designed by persons having any knowledge of the conditions prevailing at Port Nelson.	It would appear
that these scows will not prove of much practical value. Actual conditions should have been anticipated before constructing scows of this design. Another steamer despatched with cargo to Hudson bay was the Cearense. This ship, I understand, was wrecked about 20 miles from Port Nelson, and I understand was totally wrecked and the cargo wholly lost. It is charged that the wreck of the Cearense was wholly due to the lack of proper navigation aids, and which was easily avoidable. I wish to refer to statements made respecting conditions there by one or two persons who were on board the Cearense, and I do so for the purpose of giving to the House the opinion of those who had the advantage of personal observation of conditions generally. Captain Howard, of the Cearense, was interviewed at Halifax on his return, and he is reported in the Halifax Chronicle newspaper.
That is the man who lost the ship?

Yes, he was the captain of the lost ship, and he says that the loss was due to the neglect of certain employees of the Government. This paper says:
Captain Howard, the commander in charge of the ill-fated steamer at the time of the disaster, speaks only in enigmas, the following of which, given to The Morning Chronicle and signed by him, is quite characteristic of all his statements regarding the wreck of his steamer.
Captain Howard refuses any statement regarding loss of Cearense but suggests that sleepers remember that parties are awake even though those who are responsible to aids to navigation should remain abed-servants of the people, even though Government employees.
That might sound to hon. gentlemen rather enigmatic, but what Captain Howard doubtless meant was that had proper assistance been rendered by other Government vessels there his ship would not have been lost. The steamer Acadia was provided with wireless apparatus and, Captain Howard alleges, had there been proper attention paid by those on board- *
Did not he have wireless?

Yes, he had wireless, but he could not get into communication with the Acadia because, as he says, the operators on the Acadia would not respond. While I am referring to the steamer Cearense, I would like to read a written statement furnished to a Halifax newspaper by one of the officers of this ship. His name is Mr. Joseph Anderson. This statement refers to conditions generally, and I would like to give it to the House. It is as follows:
In writing this article the facts and statements are taken while the steamer Beothic is lying at Port Nelson to be unloaded. The conditions as follows, are not the least bit exaggerated : Whilst aboard the steamer Beothic one could cast his eye across the Nelson river and meet with a sight of great distress, as some of the near-lying vessels which had been anchored from two to three months, were compelled to leave with the best part of their cargo on board, knowing that the bay, within another month, would freeze, and thus all chances of leaving would be lost. The cargo of lumber that the steamer Alcazar and the steamer Alette carried upon their forward and after decks, was thrown overboard, as this was their only salvation.
One could see 12 by 12 lumber, and all kinds of spars and logs floating down the bay. The whole cause of this situation is the inadequate system of handling freight.
Further, he says:
If ever conditions were in a state of remorse, things are certainly at their worst in the handling of provisions and the housing of the workmen at Port Nelson. On arriving on shore, the eye meets with such a spectacle that one can hardly believe that such a condition really exists. Food and provisions in every shape and form can be found lying in heaps, at the mercy of all weathers,.-like coal, heaped upon an open field,-only the more perishable goods, such as flour, &c., being protected by heavy canvas. This means that there are thousands of dollars worth of provisions that are found utterly useless within the period of a week or two, and condemned to the scrap pile.
He proceeds further, but I shall not give to the House the concluding part of his statement. However, such is the opinion expressed by one who was there and who personally observed the conditions. I wish also at this moment to read a portion of a statement made to the Halifax Chronicle by Mr. Page who, I think, was employed upon another, steamer but who, of course, had knowledge of actual conditions. I do not propose reading it all, but a portion only, and which is as follows:-
If they ever make a port of Port Nelson, they want a different class of men up there than they have today. They want a master

mind who will be able to direct affairs, who will have the knowledge of what is required, and who has had experience in building decks and marine equipment under the most trying conditions, for those at Port Nelson are sufficient to tax the power of any man. As it is now, the work is handled by men not much more than students. .	.	. One of the most
striking evidences of the incompetency and ' don't care ' attitude of the authorities is connected with the wrecked steamer Cearense. She struck in shoal water and almost every bit of her cargo could have been saved had there been any one present with enough interest to make the least effort to recover any portion of the valuable material she had aboard. As it is she lies there, every day meaning further damage, the waves and ice breaking asunder her hull and scattering her cargo. As proof that much of this machinery and provisions stored in her could have been salved, is the fact that sufficient of the wireless equipment was procured to enable the port to have communication with the Pas during the winter if they get it erected.
I believe the wireless equipment was saved by a representative of Lloyds, who went from New York to Hudson bay specially in connection with the wreck of the Cearense.
It was of course necessary to have a towboat to convey laden vessels and materials eight or nine miles up the Nelson river to the location of the proposed terminals. The Department of Railways purchased the tug Kathleen, at Halifax, and for which there was paid the sum of ten thousand dollars. This is the information contained in the answer to a question asked by me.
The answer given to the question distinctly says that the Kathleen was bought after public advertisement calling for tenders. We certainly could not be in collusion with any one as to her purchase.
I have no recollection of that being a portion of the answer.
I have a copy of the answer right here.

I have no doubt that the minister is correct. A powerful tugboat was needed, and the businesslike method to pursue in such a case would be to secure a tug sufficiently powerful and efficient for the purpose. I assert that the steamer Kathleen was totally unfit for the service, and nobody in connection with the Department of Railways should have shown such utter lack of judgment as to have purchased her for that work. I trust the minister was not personally responsible for it. A word or two further about the steamer Kathleen. There is a current of

about eight or nine knots an hour in the Nelson .river.
That is exaggerated.

I doubt if it is
exaggerated. That statement is made by persons who have personal knowledge of the conditions there. The steamer Kathleen was capable of making about nine knots, and when in use in Nova Scotia carrying lobster boats, it is said she could make about two miles an hour with a very light tow. It is quite obvious, therefore, that the steamer Kathleen in attempting to tow a heavily laden scow up this current to the port terminals could not possibly make any headway whatever. In fact she would make progress backwards. If given sufficient time she might find herself going through Hudson straits and out into the Atlantic, rather than up the Nelson river.
That is exaggerated too.

That is, perhaps, a little exaggerated, because the captain in charge of the Kathleen would take means to prevent that. It is quite clear, however, that very weak judgment was exercised in purchasing this steamer. It is the opinion of every person capable of expressing an opinion on the matter, that the Kathleen was unsuitable for the purpose for which she was bought.
The information which reached the public concerning the conduct of affairs at Hudson bay during the past season came from those who were there, and who submitted themselves to newspaper interviews. A very full and comprehensive statement was given to a Halifax newspaper by Captain Robertson, of the steamer Alette, with reference to the conditions as he found them, and concerning the project generally. Captain Robertson is a very competent and intelligent man, and was, I think, personally interested in a favourable outcome of the undertaking. I crave the indulgence of hon. gentlemen if I read rather copiously from his statement. I desire to put it on record, and if Captain Robertson is a reputable and trustworthy man, the facts should be before the House and the public. In his statement, which appears in the Halifax Chronicle of Tuesday, November 5, Captain Robertson, in discussing the whole matter, gives his experience in the Hudson bay:
Our great difficulty was that the aids to navigation did not agree with the charts furnished
43i
us at Halifax before proceeding north. The channel is very adequately and accurately charted, hut the Marine Department have failed to place buoys where the charts signify. The only buoys placed there are small iron barrels that I believe have been placed there by the Acadia. The channel is marked to be buoyed and certain buoys said to exist that are not there and never were there to my knowledge. This is openly the fault of the Marine Department, showing evident carelessness on their part. The big buoys were suggested and recommended by Captain Anderson and the Government charts show them, but they have never been placed in position, neither are they up there.
I have heard words of commendation expressed by persons who were at Hudson bay last season concerning the hydrographic work performed by the steamer Acadia, and I think it is only fair that I should make this statement. But I have-heard very serious criticism of the Marine and Fisheries Department for their failure to carry out the recommendations of the Hydrographic Board. Proceeding, he said:
These small barrel buoys have a flagstaff with a piece of rag tied to the top of them. With regard to that leading buoy it is marked on the chart, but it is not in the position indicated. In fact was not in existence, which again is the fault of the Marine Department or whoever your Government has to look after such matters, for I understand that the Acadia's duty was not to place these buoys, but only to chart them, and it was up to the Marine Department to see that they were properly placed. As I was trying to find the channel, the steamer Cearense lying to the port of us nearly piled us up on the ledge where she was stranded. Not knowing that she was aground I attempted to come around near her, but hit the bank. We were fortunately not going with much speed, so I forced down the helm and steered off to the starboard. There Is no doubt to my mind that the leading buoy not being in position was the cause of the Cearense being wrecked. Had there been a conspicuous buoy marking the outer end of the channel, or what is generally termed the fairway, the accident would very likely not have occurred. Had the buoy been there a valuable ship and a valuable cargo would have been saved.
I suppose it is only fair that I should say that any criticism which is made by Captain Robertson in regard to the placing of the buoys is not properly directed against the Minister of Railways, whose department is blameless, but against the Marine and Fisheries Department, which neglected to place buoys recommended by the officers on the steamer Acadia, and which should have been placed before the Government undertook the responsibility of sending valuable ships and cargoes to traverse the waters of Hudson bay. Captain Robertson proceeds to discuss his own experience in navigating Hudson bay. It

will be remembered that he was the captain of the steamer Alette which went there, timber laden, and was obliged to return to Sydney with its Cargo undischarged, except a small portion which he threw overboard.
He did not return.

The minister is right and I am wrong. There were so many ships in the Hudson bay fleet that it is hard to keep in mind the names. Captain Robertson says:
About a couple of hours alter we arrived that beautiful tug Kathleen came down with Mr. McLaughlin, the engineer of the construction work, accompanied by Captain Fleetly, marine superintendent, on board. I served notice on them of being ready to discharge the cargo at 9 a.m. the next day and that X would count lay days from that date. We were then anchored eight miles from the site of the town which was as close as advisable for a steamer of the Alette's draft to get and where vessels of her size could lay. The Alcazar and Beothic were both lying near, one above us and the other below, Mr. McLaughlin looked over the scows and wanted to know how long before I would be ready to discharge them. X informed him as soon as the deck cargo was off the ship. The engineer then left, but came next day, again looking over the ship, went back to the camp, and returned that evening giving instructions to throw the deck load overboard so that he could see the scows. When he saw the scows after the deck load had been thrown overboard and partially lost and destroyed in the currents and tides, he came to the conclusion that the scows would be of no use to him in Port Nelson that year. After that he simply ignored us, never coming to the ship unless we sent for him. I urged him to allow us to discharge the cargo so we could get out before the ice blocked the passage. He was always making promises. He had not the means with which to perform them. He was continually promising to send men and lighters when he had only one lighter, the Neophyte. This lighter is an old motor schooner. She has a capacity of 200 tons.
I pointed out to Mr. McLaughlin as soon as I learned the true state of affairs that it was [DOT]dangerous for the Alette to remain, that it endangered not only the ship, but the lives of the men as well, and I asked him to let me sail. As far as the cargo was concerned they wanted provisions and stores more than they needed the lumber and piling with which the Alette was filled, for her cargo was not required there for a long time. I urged that, as long as we lay there, but was as persistently refused. Had it not been for Captain Saunders, Lloyds surveyor, who had come up on the Bellaventure, approaching him-
That is, Mr. McLaughlin-
__on the subject, he would have kept us there
until I would have been compelled to have taken the matter into my own hands and sailed to save the lives of my men and myself. By this time the ship was not in any too good condition owing to the damage done to the bottom of the ship by striking against the boulders which cover the bed of the Nelson river. These

boulders are the greatest danger to anything with a draught of over eighteen feet. On the evening of October 4 I received instructions from Mr. McLaughlin to sail. It took me until the 7 th to secure that portion of the deck load which still remained on the ship.
Now, I wish to refer to his criticism of the scow, sent for lightering purposes to Hudson bay:
Here I want to refer to the scows and the absolutely inadequate design of them for the work they were supposed to perform. It was nothing more than the idea of a jackass that would have provided such a thing for service in Port Nelson. They were great, huge, massive affairs, perfectly square, whereas the only thing that could ever navigate that river against those tides and currents should be built pointed with a bow and a helm that would answer readily. These were sent up with us in sections and were to be put together for the Kathleen, that beautiful little tug, that was built for pulling lobster pots around to tow up and down the river. We did get one of the sections overboard, but it sunk soon after we launched it. We then discovered that the scows could never have been properly put together at Port Nelson, for the only facflitiep for clinching a rivet is one old blacksmith, his son and a portable anvil.
This, if Captain Robertson is correct, is but additional evidence of the general lack of preparation on the part of Department of Railways. He proceeds to discuss conditions as he found them on shore. He says:
Piled high on shore you would find mixed in heaps, ropes, chains, boxes of provisions, Big Ben clocks, boxes of cigarettes and cigarette papers, and tins of milk. I cannot remember the stuff, but there were piles of it of all descriptions, some covered by tafpaulins, some had become uncovered by the wind, and there were piles of provisions over which nothing had been put.	*
He then refers to the provision made for housing the men and which he criticises rather severely. I wish to read further his remarks as to the provision made for landing facilities:
The facilities at Port Nelson consist of a small wharf like a fisherman's landing, not anything more. On this staging there is erected a small derrick capable of handling not more than five tons. The Neophyte ties up alongside of it with her load and as the tide goes down, sinks with it until left on the bottom. She then has to wait until the tide returns before she can leave the wharf to go back to the ship for another load.
Discussing the propriety of the project in a general way, he says:
The proposal to navigate Hudson bay may be a very good one, but at Port Nelson there is no possibility of ever making a port of shelter for ships, if finding too much ice in the straits, they return to port for the winter. From what I know of Fort Churchill it seems much more likely a place. Then, again, in the construe-

tion of any port at Hudson bay, there is need of engineers who have had practical experience in building ports in the most difficult places. Gold medallists may know how to mix concrete, but there is something more than that needed at Port Nelson to-day if there is ever to he anything done.
I am sorry to have occupied so much of the time of the House in reading the statement made by Captain Robertson, but 'inasmuch as he appears to discuss the question in a very comprehensive way, and in the light of his personal experience, I thought it desirable to give his views to the House, and have them placed on ' Hansard.' The assertions of Captain Robertson, which agree thoroughly with those made by others who were at Hudson bay during the summer, indicate, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, an utter lack of business methods in connection with the work carried on at Hudson bay last summer by the Department of Railways. Suitable or ample provisions clearly were not made by the Government for receiving the numerous valuable cargoes sent there for the purpose of the construction of the port terminals. It is difficult indeed to understand how any department of the Government, particularly the one presided over by the Minister of Railways, could have overlooked the provision of adequate facilities for lightering the cargoes from ships. I think the fact that the steamer Kathleen was the only steamer purchased and sent to the Hudson bay as a tow-boat is open to very grave censure indeed. On the whole, I submit that I have given the House sufficient evidence to indicate that the operations carried on last season in Hudson bay are scarcely creditable to the country or to the Government. I think the result has been, and will so prove in the future, to be quite damaging to the Hudson Bay railway project in the eyes of Canadians generally. If the establishment of a terminal port in the Hudson bay is possible, and is eventually selected, it will for quite a time be prejudiced by reason of the conditions prevailing at Port Nelson last season.
I do not propose to refer further to these matters at any great length, but, as I said in the beginning of my remarks, the question naturally arises whether a proper selection was made when Port Nelson was designated as the port terminal for the projected Hudson Bay railway. I do not propose discussing the advisability of the construction of the railway itself; that is a matter of public policy to which Parliament has long been committed. It is, however, very important that the best available port be
selected as the terminal of the railway. I will not attempt to urge upon the Government that in selecting Port Nelson a mistake was made. I would not present myself as a competent judge of such a matter. I do say, however, that the selection of a terminal port is a matter of extreme importance, and because of the experience of last season the selection of Port Nelson for the railway terminal is at least open to some question. I do trust that we shall have from the minister some statement indicating the reasons which led him to recommend to the Government the selection of Port Nelson. We should, I am sure, be very glad to hear from him particularly by reason of the fact that he has made a personal investigation. There is a great deal of evidence to the effect that Fort Churchill is the more desirable port. I have in my hand a published statement of one William Beech, of Winnipeg, who is reputed to have spent a great part of his life in the Hudson bay country. I have no personal knowledge as to his competency to give an opinion as to the desirability of selecting either port, but-
I think he would be more capable of giving an opinion as to the townsite which he owns at Fort Churchill.

At any rate, there is a portion of his statement which I desire to read, because it. agrees very thoroughly with the assertions made by some of the captains of steamers who were in the Hudson bay during the past season.
By that I mean that he is a prejudiced witness.

speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK COCHRANE (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman led off by saying that the House had never been favoured with an expression of opinion or an explanation why Nelson was selected. If I remember correctly, and I have not looked up ' Hansard,' I gave the reasons last session. The hon. member has truly said that I went up there in 1912. I looked at both harbours, not for one moment thinking that I am a harbour engineer or an expert in navigation. When we arrived at Nelson first we looked over the situation, and I must say, frankly and freely, as I did then, that it is not an ideal harbour. On going up to Churchill and looking at it we found that it was not ideal either, although in regard to expense it could be created a harbour a good deal cheaper than Port Nelson. One strong reason influencing us is that there is 70 miles of barren lands which we would have to cross to go to Churchill. This tract has been frozen since Adam was a kid and I have yet to meet an engineer who will vouch for the building of a road across that 70 miles. As all people know, railroads when built should be ditched in order to carry off the surface water and it can be imagined what the result of building a road through such land would be. Taking that into consideration, no engineer would advise building across that country. There was no other place for us to develop but Nelson. Another great reason for that is that this will be a grain road to a great extent; it is 85 miles shorter to Nelson than to Churchill. It will cost more to develop Nelson.
One objection I have to the criticism of the hon. gentleman is that he has collected the opinions of men who were either interested or who had had mishaps, either through their own neglect or negligence or

accidents that could not be helped. I may say that the steamer Cearense is a total loss owing to it3 own captain. They arrived there some time in the evening. They anchored out quite a distance and alongside of the Marine and Fisheries boat Acadia. They communicated with the boat that night. The captain started off in the morning without asking the captain of the Acadia to give him any information about going in. I understand, further from our own people that the Cearenses' wireless was out of commission and to prove that two of the captains of the ships that were in Nelson harbour have told me that they tried to communicate with him in order to inform him that he was taking the wrong direction. He went on without taking any soundings at all, because had he done so he would have found that he was in very shallow water. He did not go where the buoys were and I am absolutely without fear of contradiction in the statement that this man was altogether at fault for the losing of the ship.
In 1912 we sent an engineer and party up to look over the situation, and bring down plans to show us what was needed. We employed Mr. Hazen for the purpose. He went up by the Beothic, landing there in August and he came down in the winter, I think in February. He brought his plans down. The chief engineer of the department, who has been there a long time and in whom I have absolute confidence, did not agree with the layout proposed by Mr. Hazen and after a long distance discussion Mr. Hazen said that if he could not have his way in reference to the laying out of the scheme he would not go back. But he said he would stay and see to it that the things they needed, both in the way of lighters, supplies and materials would be shipped up. He did stay, he was in charge of the loading of all of these things and of the engaging of the boats, and he went up with them. I may say that the scows, to which reference has been made, were to have been delivered at Halifax by the first of July. The makers, unfortunately, like a lot of other manufacturers, were away behind in filling the order, but we sent them up as soon as possible. We loaded the greater portion of the merchandise on the steamer Beothic which was going up for the Marine Department, and just to show the luck we had, I might say that she struck on a rock off the coast of Newfoundland and had to be put in dry dock at Halifax. We
have not been able to communicate with him, as we expected to, by wireless this winter. We hope, however, in a few days to receive the first message. The Cearense took up what apparatus was not carried by the Beothic, and the installation of the wireless was completed about the first of December. In reference to the harbour, we purchased a dredge which we proposed to use in the spring. We employed the best men we could get in order to get the dredge up there safely. The best man recommended was Captain Saunders, who was Lloyd's inspector in New York. He' went up there personally, and in a report which he sent me, he says in reference to the Nelson river:
The condition of Nelson river as compared with other swift rivers, such as the Mississippi, Delaware, Mersey, Thames, Hoogly, Moulmain, etc., from my own personal experience, X am satisfied that the navigation and anchorages in the above-mentioned rivers are far more dangerous and difficult to navigate than the Nelson river.
With regard to the timber, I may say that we never intended to lighter it in. Mr. Hazen recommended that it could be rafted in. He tried that and failed, although he took boom chains up for the purpose of making a boom out of the long pieces of timber by means of which the timber was to be taken in, but he never attempted it. I do not know why, he has never made a report. It was never, however, our intention to lighter in this timber.
In reference to the Alette, I may say that Captain Freakley, who has had
4	p.m. 15 years experience in those waters, tells me that if Captain Robertson's boat was hurt in the Nelson river, it was through his own fault. His explanation is that Robertson gave his boat too much chain-something over 90 fathoms -while swinging to the tide at slack water. The other captains used two chains. He tells me that Robertson was advised to do this, but did not take the advice and met with an accident. Later, when re-entering Nelson river with the Acadia following her into port as a convoy, Captain Robertson, for reasons not yet explained, turned his vessel about and ran her aground. There was about 20 feet depth of water at low tide in the river channel opposite the dock site. I may say the steamer Minto has been up, opposite to where the terminals are being built, without any accident. But these big boats absolutely refused to go up that far and I do not blame them very much. They

could have gone with perfect safety, how* ever, but the captains were afraid. In reference to not having facilities at Port Nelson for handling this freight, my hon. friend should think for a moment. We only had a survey party there. We cannot get timber to build a dock by the river, unless we go about 100 miles, and then it is very scarce. We had no horses to haul timber. We had either to do one thing or the other, and we thought it best to get this timber in so as to have a long season next year. The season this year was very short. The first steamer did not arrive there until August, as it was hindered by ice. We expected it to get there by the middle of July, as the boat got off in good time. All the ships were unloaded with the exception of the Alette and the Alcazar. As my hon. friend has stated, the Alcazar was chartered to go to Hudson bay, and it is a question whether we could not even now insist on their going back with the timber. As to that, I will not express any opinion.
Mr. McLaughlin, who succeeded Mr. Hazen, is a man who has been in the department for a long time. I think he is a live young man. He may have had more than he could possibly handle, but I have not lost any faith in him or in the port. They got off a good deal of the timber, enough to build a dock for the lighters. They also landed their engines and the track and were able to handle the stuff. We hope to send a large number of men overland this winter, in order to get a full summer's work done next season. If we took them up by steamer we could not expect to land there until the end of July at the earliest. I may say that we were very unfortunate in not getting those scows. They would have furnished ample lightering, according to the engineers. We have had considerable difficulty this year, but we must expect that in connection with the ports in that northern country. Everything has to be taken in, before we can construct anything. The big dredge that was sent in was not wrecked. Captain Saunders was good enough to take some photographs, and I have one here showing the dredge high and dry. I am quite sure we have made no mistake in the selection of men, and we feel we will get a good year's work done in the coming summer, and that we shall have sufficient dockage and the dredging well advanced when the road reaches Port Nelson. It will not be finished by any means, because if the strait is a success, we shall have to spend

an enormous amount of money in carrying out the scheme. I still have great hopes that the changes which have taken place in the St. Lawrence will also take place in the Hudson strait. I do not feel that we are entitled to any censure. We may have made some mistakes; we only had a short time to get in these things, and we got in as much as ever we could. We have got enough provisions in there to carry on the men till next summer, and I am quite satisfied that the results of another year will be pleasing not only to myself but to the House and the country as well.

I am sure the statement that has been made by the minister is full justification for the motion and criticism of my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean). This is a matter of very great importance upon which the public should be informed, and in regard to which there should be no delay in giving the fullest information. I am very pleased with the attitude of the minister towards the question in hand. I accept his position as being entirely friendly to the project and I accept unreservedly the statement of his intentions to push it to completion as rapidly as possible. But, at the same time, where an enterprise is of such far reaching importance as this Hudson Bay railway, where it affects such a large number of the people of Canada and affects so directly what I claim is the most important interest of the people of Canada, anything that does, or seems to, throw discredit upon that project must necessarily be the subject of criticism and possibly of adverse criticism.
I need not say to the House-it has been said before and it will be echoed by all the representatives from the prairie west-that in the opinion of the people of that country, the future progress and welfare of the West is in large measure dependent upon the successful development of a transportation route by way of Hudson's bay and that any delay in the accomplishment of that object is a serious detriment to the welfare of that country, and, therefore, to the whole country. It must, therefore, be accepted that they look with hostility upon any action, or any failure to act, that may delay the completion of the enterprise or may discredit it to any serious extent.
In regard to the choice of the port of Nelson, as against that of Churchill, we have this situation, that there is beyond question a port at Churchill which answers every requirement resulting from the con-

struction of a railway to that port at a minimum cost for port development. The objections stated by the minister, are, first, that the road to Churchill would be increased in length some 85 miles, and would traverse for a considerable distance barren or frozen ground not suitable for railway construction, that there would be the extra cost for that additional 85 miles, and of course, the additional cost of the operation of that 85 miles. These are matters that are fair to be taken into consideration. As far as my hon. friend's objection, or the objection of his engineers, to the possibility of building to Churchill over that frozen ground is concerned, I do not think that the contention-

Probably I forgot to
mention that there are about nine feet of moss and muck and stuff of that kind, deeper at some points than at others. By ditching the right of way at each side and carrying off the water and letting the wind and air into it, it might be possible to make a change in the condition of that material.

The experience in the
Yukon is that, when the first wagon roads were being built, the builders were careful to avoid the low ground; they carried the roads over the tops of hills in order to keep to the dry ground, but since that time they have built wherever the levels were most favourable and roads have been carried through muskegs. The ground, being permanently frozen, provides an absolutely solid foundation which is as secure as if it were solid rock, and roads built in that way have proved most satisfactory.

You are referring to
traffic roads?

I believe that the conditions which apply to the one would hold good in regard to the other. I am putting that forward as the experience in the Yukon and therefore I maintain that the contention of my hon. friend does not hold. As to the length of the road, as to the capital expenditure that will be involved in the construction of that road and as to the cost of operation, if Port Nelson can be constructed and equipped for less money, or for an amount of money equal to that which it would cost to build the additional mileage to Churchill, I say, certainly, Nelson is the proper choice.
But it Ts just possible that the cost of establishing a satisfactory port at Nelson will really be greater than the cost of the construction of the 85 miles of extra railway
line and it is possible that the maintenace of that port when constructed will cost more than the construction and operation of these 85 miles. That may seem to be an extreme statement about conditions at the mouth of Nelson river. My hon. friend speaks of an engineer who has had experience in regard to ports at the mouths of many rivers of the world. I will venture to say that in not a single one of these cases is the condition approximately similar to that at the mouth of the Nelson river.
This man spoke from his own experience. He was not an engineer, he was a navigator and his experience was applicable to this case.

I think that what he spoke of was the port after it was created, not the condition as it exists at the present time. There is no similarity between the conditions at the mouth of the Nelson river and those at the mouths of any of the rivers that he has mentioned. I do not condemn the selection of Port Nelson on that account-not at all, but I think the Government has scarcely appreciated the serious character of the work that will be required to make Nelson a satisfactory port.
We certainly have.

I think they scarcely
appreciate the amount of work or the expenditure that will be necessary. It would appear to me that the mishaps of the present season afford evidence that the Government did not appreciate the difficulties they had to face. Beginning many years ago, examinations have been made at the mouth of the Nelson river, and they have been continued from time to time. The Government had the whole of the season of 1912 to inform itself regarding the difficulties to be encountered. Hon. gentlemen will remember a discussion in the House when the Government was criticised very severely, even by some of its own supporters, because work on the Hudson Bay railroad had been stopped for a time, and in the session of 1911-12 it was filially announced that the policy of the Government was to build the railway and to select the terminal port as soon as possible. The Minister of Railways himself visited Hudson bay in 1912, and yet in 1913 an expedition was sent up to begin the great work of establishing a port at Nelson, which expedition ended largely in disaster and disappointment.

Oh, no. I must take exception to that. There were only two

ships that had any trouble, and I have shown that it was their own fault. The other ships had no trouble, and two of them made two trips each without encountering any difficulty.
How many ships went up?
Six.
The loss of one of the ships-
The loss was completely covered by .insurance.
Oh, yes.
Then, it is not a loss.

It is not a financial loss, but I am speaking of the loss of the ship, and the bringing back of one of the cargoes, to say nothing of the reports that have been published as to the destruction of supplies, and the admission of the minister himself that the wireless apparatus arrived there only in part, and that for that reason he has not ibeen able to get into communication with the port.

I said we were unfortunate that the principal part of the wireless was put on the Beothic, which had an accident along the coast of Newfoundland and had to go back. Some of the apparatus went by another of the ships, and we got that landed there.
That part of the wireless apparatus was saved by the salvage company.
No; there was no salvage company up there at all.
That was the statement made by my hon. friend (Mr. A. K. Maclean).
I know, but he made a lot of statements that were not right.

The statement I made was that part of the wireless equipment had been saved by the representative of Lloyds who was up there, and that it might have been saved by some of the employees of the steamer Acadia, if they had just made a little effort.

It was saved by
people employed by the Government up there, who took it off the steamer, and not by any one sent up there for that purpose.
I take my information from the statements made by captains who were there.
By captains who were in trouble and had to give some reason fo* getting into trouble.
Perhaps the officials of the Department of Railways are in trouble and are trying to get out of trouble.
Oh, no.

I am glad to know that
the conditions are better than they have been reported.
They certainly are.
But giving the minister credit for the very best, from his own statement to-day, it cannot be said that the work at Hudson bay last summer was a startling success.
If you take the conditions into consideration I think the operations were successful.

Much as I do not wish to disagree with the minister, I am sorry to hear 'him say that, because it indicates that he and the Government do not appreciate the magnitude of the task they have undertaken. They do not seem to be fully alive to the adoption of the best means for carrying out that task with the rapidity and perfection which the enterprise requires. The tendency on the part of the Government and its engineers, has been to minimize the importance of this work. Because of a choice having to be made between Churchill and Nelson, it has been sought evidently to minimize the cost and difficulty of making the harbour at Nelson. If it is to be at Nelson, let it be at Nelson, but let it be understood that it is no boy's job to make a port at Nelson.
That is true.

The Government must
take hold of the work as a great enterprise. The country cannot afford that the Government should tinker with it and bring to bear upon it means and expenditures that are not adequate, and which not being taken with due foresight, result in loss, and damage, and delay, and discredit to the enterprise. There is no doubt that the reports which have been circulated in regard to the lack of success of the expedition of last summer have had the effect of creating a very bad impression in the public mind with regard to the practicability of the route. That is felt by every man in the prairie west as something that affects his personal interest, and it is for that reason that I dwell very strongly upon the matter. I maintain that the Government

had ample time to take due precautions with regard to the buoying of the channel, and with regard to arriving at a conclusion as to exactly what kind of vessels would be required, and what kind of material was necessary. That the Government failed to arrive at sound conclusions is demonstrated by the result. I am not suggesting that it is because of any lack of good will on the part of the minister;
I am suggesting that it is because of a desire to minimize the difficulty and expense. This is an enterprise with which the future welfare of the prairie West is absolutely bound up. The completion of the Hudson Bay railway and the inauguration of the Hudson bay route cuts practically 1,000 miles of interior transportation out of the cost of delivery of grain by that route, between the West and Liverpool. Such a cut in the cost of transportation is worth an incalculable amount. It might mean the difference between success and failure, in a given state of the wheat market, for the men who are producing in the Prairie West. So that it is of the utmost importance that every step taken towards the accomplishment of this enterprise shall be taken with due forethought, with due judgment and with a due appreciation of the necessity that the route shall not be a failure and shall not create the impression that it is a failure. It is not that I am urging undue haste; I am not urging that the road should be completed this year, or next year or the year after. What I am urging is that the Government shall take due time, shall use due forethought, shall use sound judgment, and shall be prepared to make the necessary expenditures-not slackening the work, but so proceeding that when the road is completed there shall be a satisfactory port established and equipped to transact the business of the road, and so that the route may be a success once it is opened and the expenditure upon it thereby made profitable. There are many interests and many prejudices against this route, and I need not say that when the road is completed to the bay, if the port facilities are not as they ought to be it will take very little to establish in the minds of the public at large a prejudice against that route that will take years to overcome. It is absolutely necessary that nothing should be done, that no chances should be taken, to allow such a prejudice to be formed. It is because of this that I speak of it and criticise the minister for the condition of the enterprise of last summer and the results that have been
achieved. The road is under construction. It is not being pushed with great rapidity, but we are told that about one-third of the total length is now graded, and some 80 miles actually under steel. At that rate of progress, and certainly it is not a rapid rate, the road will reach Port Nelson before that port is fit to handle the business, judged by the progress of last summer. I would be glad to see the work on the road proceeding more rapidly than it is now, but I urge still more strongly that the port facilities shall be completed by the time the road reaches Port Nelson. Otherwise, the route and the enterprise will receive injury from which it will take it years to recover.
Mr. J. A. M. AIKINS (Brandon); I should consider myself remiss in my duty to Western Canadians if I did not express on this occasion our gratitude to the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) for his prompt and energetic action in respect of the Hudson Bay railway and the Hudson bay route. Something is being done. The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has made the statement that he would not like to urge on the Minister of Railways undue haste in the construction of this harbour. I imagine that when he was sitting on this side of the House as Minister of the Interior he was perhaps saying to the then Minister of Railways the same thing-that he did not wish to urge undue haste; and certainly they did not make it. If the advice of the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) were taken, that we should take very cautious steps one after another, year after year, then the Hudson bay harbour might be built, perhaps, when the millennium arrives. Any misadventures that have arisen during the year have arisen out of the prompt and energetic action of the minister, who did not wish delay. But
The best-laid schemes of mice an' men Gang aft agley,
it has been said. The statement of the minister has shown that he took every possible precaution to have the expeditions that went put last year to Hudson bay a success. It was not because the arrangements were not properly made, but because the human equations did not work out right. For instance, the scows did not arrive in time, and other plant was not constructed in time, and so when these vessels came up to Nelson there had

not been earried out by some persons the arrangements which the minister had very wisely made. Had they been carried out, there would have been no such accidents or misadventures. I do not intend to dwell further on this point, but I will say that I do not think the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) made out even a prima facie case against the minister. He read to us statements made by Mr. Beach, who, it was well known, is interested as one of the townsite owners at Churchill, and who, naturally, would favour the idea of the terminus being at Churchill. Then he read statements from newspapers, not verified in any way. If we are to accept statements contained in the papers, it seems to me we shall have a very poor basis for action by this House.
In respect of the harbour itself, the late Government let a contract for the Hudson Bay railway, at least the first part of it commencing at the Pas, but they did not then know where it was to terminate. It had a loose end-'which might be anywhere from Newfoundland to the North Pole.
Don't be extravagant, now. Newfoundland as a terminus for a Canadian railway is stretching it, rather.
Over toward the bay of Fundy, then, we will say.
They are not very close together.

In following the remarks of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), I understood that he was speaking not of the expedition with which the railway might be constructed, per se, but rather of the question as to which should be completed first, the railway or the harbour improvements. I think the hon. member for Brandon took my hon. friend up wrong when he endeavoured to create the impression that the hon. member for Edmonton had said that he was in no hurry for the railway. What the hon. member for Edmonton did say was, that in any event, even if only very moderate progress were made, the railway should toe completed at least as soon as the harbour improvements. I think it goes without saying that the railway in itself is of no use until the harbour improvements are effected.
The hon. member for Brandon, as he usually does when he has a very weak case, endeavours to make some disparaging remarks with regard to the Government that went out of office in September, 1911. My hon. friend is an old and eminent practitioner at the Bar, and it is probably not the first time that, finding his own case weak, he has endeavoured to lend it a spurious strength by abusing the other side and introducing into the discussion matters entirely irrelevant. That is exactly what he is endeavouring to do in this case. I may tell the hon. member that the late Government is not guilty of the irrelevant charge that he brings in against it-because, I say, it is irrelevant; it has nothing to do with the responsibility of the present Government or the gentleman who holds the portfolio of Railways and Canals. However, even if it were not irrelevant, the Government is not guilty of the accusation brought against it by the hon. member for Brandon. It is true that during all the years the late Government was in office, requests were made of them from time to time that the Hudson Bay railway should be undertaken as a matter of government policy. Some years after I became a member of this House the matter was still a moot point, although neither party in this House was committed to it. Resolutions were moved by private members; the matter was spoken to by the leaders on both sides of the House, and in the course of time-I think it was in the year 1908-the late Government for the first time declared itself as being committed to the policy of the construction of the Hudson Bay railway. After that year the Government remained in power a little less than three years, and, in view of the number of preliminary steps that were necessary, I submit that there was no great

delay in entering upon the carrying out of this project. Within three years the project was well under way, and a substantial part of the construction of the railway had been let to the J. D. McArthur Company. The hon. member for Brandon, referring to the attitude of the Liberals and my hon. friend the member for Edmonton with regard to the matter, spoke sarcastically of what he termed their undue haste. Since he has taken upon himself to say that there was no undue haste in this matter, I wonder why the Government does not employ a little more haste in connection with the Hudson Bay railway? They have been in office quite a while now, and are practically no further ahead-that is the unfortunate part of it. The grain growers on the prairies are not looking at this question to-day as the hon. member for Brandon does; they are not comparing the attitude of the late Government with that of the present Administration-about that they do not care a rap. They look at it not from a partisan standpoint, but from the viewpoint of men who want the railway built and the harbour improvements effected as soon as possible so that they can get. their grain out. They are not concerned with the rhetoric of the hon. member for Brandon, nor with his scoffing at the late Administration.
These men in the constituency of Brandon wish that their representative would do what he could to urge* the Government to really get down to work and get this railway built and in operation to carry out their wheat, 60 pounds to the bushel. The grain growers are in a bigger hurry for this than they are for any great sum to be spent or squandered on navies; they are in a bigger hurry for this even than they are for free wheat, although the hon. member for Brandon, I think, will walk arm and arm with me on the wheat question before the session is much older. We will see whether he will come along with us. If he has the interests of his constituents at heart he will show some of his undue haste in the alacrity with which he will ally himself with the Liberal party on free wheat. The farmers of the West are desirous of having the railway built; but they wish this Government to first carefully consider what should be the proper policy to adopt and then get down to practical work and carry that policy to fruition. If there is anything the hon. member for Brandon can do to aid the Government, well and good; but if he cannot do that, let him at least urse the Gov-
[Mr. Knowles. I
emment that they must satisfy the demand of the grain growers of the prairies and get the road built; because all the people of Canada, irrespective of politics, are committed to this as a great national enterprise, now, no matter What the differences of opinion may have been in the past.
The Government seem to be very sure that they have given us good reasons for going to Nelson instead of to Churchill. The hon. gentleman who holds the portfolio of Railways and Canals tells us that he gave us those reasons last year. I do not think he is correct in that; I think he is under a misapprehension. I have looked through ' Hansard ' and after a careful search I do not see anything there in the way of reasons. The minister, as far as I am able to gather, never gave any real, public reason for deciding on Port Nelson, and I think his reasons dre such that he is not telling us all of them. I think the hon. member for Brandon probably could tell us more reasons than he has told us. I think if we got next a few club friends in real estate firms in Winnipeg he might get a different opinion from that of Mr. Beach.
The land is all withdrawn for one half mile on each side, so nobody can get in there; there is no real estate proposition there.
I think I am correct in saying that the land around what is supposed to be the town of Port Nelson is, some of it, taken.
That is withdrawn too.
To the extent of two miles.
Your Government sold the lots at Fort Churchill.
We are not dealing with that now. There was evidently nothing wrong about it or it would have been brought up in this House long before. It was not like the Donaldson homestead, anyway.
I may say that there was no land sold at Fort Churchill by the late Government or while the late Government was in office.
My information on the subject came from the deputy of the hon. gentleman who just rose, and who was formerly Minister of the Interior.

The deputy misinformed
my hon. friend.

The Minister of the Interior answered a question on January 16, 1912, with regard to this precious land which he has withdrawn-although I tell you we will all be surprised if there are not a few good Tories who get in on that half mile, knowing them as we, know them, the Minister of the Interior to the contrary notwithstanding. I would like to get all the land the Tories will get inside that half-mile. If I had it I do not think I would have to work any more.
You will find out before you get through.

The question was asked:
Has a strip of public land one-half mile in width along the line of the Hudson Bay railway been closed against settlement?
And the answer was, ' yes.' That land was closed against settlement, according to the Minister of the Interior, before Port Nelson was finally decided upon as the terminal. That answer was given on the 14th of January, 1912.

It was decided on
then.

It was decided on then, very good. The Minister of Railways says it was decided on then, on January 14. On February 26, 1913, the Minister of Railways answered this question:
Mr. Martin (Begina) :
1.	Has the Government as yet decided upon Churchill or Nelson as the terminus of the Hudson Bay railway? If so, which point has been settled upon?	,
Mr. Cochrane:
1.	Nelson, unless upon completion of the surveys and inspection it might be thought advisable to decide otherwise.
I do not think any House of gentlemen, taking the minister seriously, would take that answer as a final answer. I think we would be only fair to the Minister of Railways and Canals if we said the answer given on the 26th of February meant that the matter was not decided, but that the Government were inclined to Nelson and were keeping their minds open in view of the probability of further information coming to them from their surveyors. If the answer did not mean that it did not mean anything, as from one fair-minded man to another. The Minister of Railways said on the 26th of February, 1913: Nelson will be the place, but we will keep our minds open, there may be some information, for he said:
Unless there be some information upon the completion of the surveys-
Mark, they have not been completed

-and explorations it might be thought advisable to do otherwise.
His mind open, there was nothing decided unless his surveys teach him differently. He was going to rest his decision on what the surveys might show. The same minister, according to his own declaration, had already told everybody that it would be Nelson. I do not think the minister will deny that. He said in February: My mind is not decided yet, because I must get further information; and months before that he had told everybody it would be Nelson.
When did I tell that ?

on the 26th of February, that this was not final yet because they had to get the surveyors' reports; but on the 4th of December of the previous year he had said: It is all settled, it is going to be Nelson. A decision made in that way is one that justifies the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) in casting the greatest suspicion upon the whole fishy business.
Which report are you in favour of ?

I am in favour of getting good information and deciding it on the merits of the case. I am not in favour of doing anything to hurt Reach, or to help Beach. I shall tell my hon. friends, and I appeal to the hon. member for Prince Albert, if he has not heard it said many times by people who have gone into this matter, that Port Nelson was chosen for some ulterior reason not given to the public. It may be the best place, I do not know. I think my hon. friend from Prince Albert (Mr. McKay) will bear me out when I say that there is a belief in the minds of many people, that all this was not done above board.

As my hon. friend has referred to me, I may say that I have heard nothing of it. So far as I know, the people are satisfied iyith the decision of the Minister of Railways, and are most gratified at the expedition with which he has taken hold of that matter.	.

As my hon. friend has referred to me, I may say that I have never heard this point discussed and the people of western Canada, at least so far as Manitoba is concerned, are quite satisfied with the decision of the minister.

I was not asking my hon. friend from Lisgar-he interrupted me -but I accept his statement without the slightest hesitation and the statement of my hon. friend from Prince Albert also, but I can tell my hon. friend from Prince Albert that I know some very great political friends of his, big men, and some of his clients, with whom I would like him to have a talk some day, just to hear the other side of the story. I am not saying that there is necessarily anything wrong in it. I do not care to make that statement as I cannot back it up, but I do say that we should have the fullest information, such as these papers call for, and that there should be an investigation. I do not say that the minister was actuated by ulterior motives in his decision. I am not going to say that, but

I do say there is enough suspicion in the minds of the people of western Canada to justify an investigation; and I think I am justified in saying that the minister decided this matter before he had full information. If he decided in December, 1912, on Port Nelson and two months later, was awaiting the report of a surveying party before making a final decision, then I say he is moving in a strange and mysterious way. If Port Nelson turns out to be the best place, it will be a lucky thing for the Government, because I believe they have gone blind into this matter. As my hon friend from Edmonton has said, it is a very expensive undertaking and of extreme importance to the people of Canada. At its commencement, it was a matter into which party politics very little entered. There was no opposition to the vote when it went through under the late Government. It seemed to be the common desire of all the people of Canada, even the people of eastern Canada, and I have never had occasion to observe any matter in this House which showed the national spirit to better advantage. All we ask is that the project be persisted in and that we may have the fullest possible light on it. The minister attributed a lot of his trouble to bad luck. Perhaps he may be lucky; and it may be that he has chosen the better place for the harbour, but if he has, it is mere luck and not after a thorough investigation of the relative merits of the two places.

My
hon. friend has isaid that polities entered into this matter very little at the outset. It was only within the last few years that the people of this country have been committed to this proposition. I remember quite well contesting a constituency in western Canada in 1904 when I was practically defeated on this proposition because the Reform party had taken it up and promised the people of western Canada that they would put the matter through. My hon. friend has said that we are no farther ahead than we were two or three years ago. Last fall I was over a portion of this road. I went over seventy miles of it, where they had the steel laid, and I want to tell this House that in my opinion it is one of the greatest pieces of work that has ever been carried on in this country; because, so far, not a single horse has been used in the construction of the road. It has all been done by hand work and you can have some idea of the work that had to be done by these

men in order to get as much done as they have at the present time. My hon. friend from Edmonton talks of tinkering with this proposition. If any proposition wi>,s ever tinkered with by any government, I am sure it is this question that was tinkered with by the Government of which ths hon member for Edmonton was a member. As to the selection of Port Nelson, I think the Government have made a very wise choice, because as my hon. friend from Brandon has said, Port Nelson is open much longer in the fall, and open much earlier in the spring than Fort Churchill. Not nly that but the railway will run pretty nearly all the way alongside the Nelson river, and in time to come there is no doubt in my mind that a very large proportion of the wheat now grown in western Canada will be milled by the power of the Nelson river. I am a great believer in the Hudson bay route. Some people tell us that it can only be navigated for two or three months out of the year. The Hudson Bay, and 5 p.m. the Hudson strait never freeze over, and the mouth of the Nelson river is open practically all the the year round; and I claim that with proper aids to navigation we shall be able to navigate' the Hudson bay and Hudson strait from eight to ten months in the year. In the early days they had a great deal more trouble navigating the St. Lawrence than they have had in navigating the Hudson bay for the last 200 or 300 years. In that time only two or three vessels have been lost in the Hudson bay and it has been navigated every year. I have read almost everything I can get my hands on, in connection with this proposition, and I believe the day will come, and is not very far distant, when 70 per cent or 80 per cent of the export wheat of western Canada will be going by this route. I believe, further, that in time ocean going vessels will be brought right up to the city of Winnipeg. I think the present minister deserves a great deal of credit, rather than censure, for the way he has handled this matter since he has taken hold of it.

1 desire to call the attention of the hon. Minister of Railways to another phase of this question, which is of considerable interest to the workingmen who live	in the
city of Halifax and who were engaged in the Government service at Port Nelson	during the past	summer.
The return of one of these steamers brought some fifty men who had been em-44
ployed in Halifax under contract with officials of the Government to work at Port Nelson. It is alleged that by their contract they were entitled to receive $3.75 a day for every day excepting Sunday after they had arrived at the scene of their employment. After being there but a short time they were made to understand that for every day, owing to unavoidable conditions of weather, they were unable to work, their pay would be kept from them, notwithstanding that their board bill continued. The consequence was that they saw no chance whatever of saving any money with the large expense they were under for board. When a change of superintendents took place they were asked to work at night instead of during the day. These men objected to that and they were told that if they were not willing to accept the altered conditions they would be taken back to Halifax. They were taken back to Halifax, and were charged $100 for their passage. Fifty-two men contributed $5,200 to the funds of the Department of Railways and Canals in respect of their transportation from Hudson bay to the city of Halifax. I do not profess to say that the Department of Railways and Canals might not have been justified under the terms of this agreement in charging these men for their transportation, but I desire to ask my hon. friend the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) to amend his motion so as to include all agreements that have been entered into between labourers in the city of Halifax and officials of the Government for the purpose of ascertaining what the rights of these men are in the premises.
The Minister of Railways and Canals endeavoured to minimize the effect of the indictment laid against his department by the junior member for Halifax by retorting across the floor that the statements which he quoted were chiefly those of the captains, who were themselves responsible for the accidents which occurred in Hudson bay, and who felt sore on account of their failure to discharge the duties which had been entrusted to them. I have before me the Canadian Courier of January 17, which contains an article signed Montague Vesey. I do not know the gentleman who contributed this article, but I am quite sure that he was neither captain, mate nor bo'sun bold upon any of these vessels chartered by the Government to go to Hudson bay. This is what Mr. Vesey says:



The work has cost one life and two ships already. The Cearense was wrecked, almost at her journey's end, and became a total loss. (Her crew and passengers had to be taken off in the lifeboats.) She is to be seen on the horizon yet, breaking up; and within a gun shot of her lies all that is left of the Alette, which, unable to make the open sea, on account of ice, returned to Nelson, ran on to a sand bar, was abandoned, and has since been totally destroyed by fire (thought to be due to combustion of gas in the bunkers).
These were the worst happenings; but ill-fortune, in a hundred minor degrees, has dogged the fpotsteps of the pioneers, from the very outset of the expedition. The Beothic went ashore on a jagged reef at Point Rich, Newfoundland, and had to sacrifice 300 tons of coal before she could be hauled off into deep water by a warship ; after which it was found necessary for her to return to Halifax, where she remained in. dry dock for a month. The Alcazar, the Alette, and the Sinbad all had to leave Port Nelson with only a portion of their cargoes unloaded, owing to the poor and fearfully inadequate facilities for discharging. The $3,000 gasolene launch brought up by the Beothic sank before she was a week in the bay; and one-half of a large steel scow, which was brought up in sections, went down within a few hours of touching the water.
