The dredge, Port Nelson, built by the Poison Iron Works (a photo of which appeared in the Courier of August 16 last), experienced such bad weather while being towed from Halifax by the Bona-venture, that it will be a long time before she can grapple with the bed of the Nelson. She lies with her back practically broken.
Where?
At Port Nelson.
Which statement is absolutely untrue.

(Reading):
Labour troubles broke out quite early in the operations, and nearly a hundred men, declining to remain any longer under existing conditions, treated their contracts as waste-paper, and demanded to be sent home on the 'Beothic' and 'Bellaventure.' This reduced the strength of the camp by nearly one-half, to say nothing of leaving the remaining half in a condition of extreme discontent. Finally, there is scarcely any oil or coal in the whole place.
The Minister of Railways and Canals interjected the observation, While I was reading this article, that there was not a word of truth in it, or something to that effect.
In reference to the fact of the dredge being broken.

Any statement that the minister 'has made, with authority as I assume, is all the more reason why the motion of my hon. friend from Halifax shoifld prevail, and that all the papers should be brought before the House. But, I believe, in view of the circumstances and in

view of the fiat denial which comes from hon. gentlemen supporting the Government as to the truth of these charges, something more than the motion of my hon. friend from Halifax as it stands today is necessary. I believe that a thorough investigation into the whole conduct of this expedition ought to be made by a select special committee of this House. My hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Aikins) intimated that in substance all these charges were made by a man named Beach, who was a real estate agent at Fort Churchill. The quotation I read is not based on the statement of any interested parties as far as I know, because my information is to the effect that Mr. Vesey went to Port Nelson for the purpose of writing up this matter and the articles which have appeared in the Halifax newspapers and the Canadian Courier are the results of his observations.
There are two or three other matters that call for some consideration at the 'hands of the members of this House. The Minister of Railways, while attempting to make a defence of this matter, only succeeded in entering a plea by way of extenuation. He stated that there was bad luck, that the conditions were not familiar to those who had undertaken to carry on the work, that the season was short and backward, and that it was impossible to anticipate the difficulties that stood in the way of the successful carrying on of this undertaking. I have been long enough a member of this House supporting the Government led by my right hon. friend who to-day leads the Opposition to have heard, day after day, charges hurled across the floor by hon. gentlemen who now sit behind the Government benches in respect of public works carried on by the late Government and in no instance did I hear of any circumstances in extenuation of what they regarded as maladministration by the late Government in the matter of these public undertakings. I merely say this for the purpose of pointing out that circumstances have changed in the last few years, and that, while hon. gentlemen allowed no extenuation in respect to what they regarded as mismanagement by the members of the late Government, they are now willing to shelter themselves behind the plea that the circumstances which led to these disasters were such as they could not control. Mr. Vesey further, in an article in the Halifax Chronicle, writes as follows:
The cause of the prevailing unrest is, in outline, thus:	It is quite clear that (luring
the severest of the winter months all outside

work, will for a great part of every week, be out of the question. But work or no work, five dollars a week has to be paid for board, and clothing has to be bought. Now, every man who possesses a contract (ninety per cent of the whole) was under the impression when he signed It, that he was to receive his pay for every day in the twelve [DOT] months; exclusive of Sundays.
That, in fact, is what the agreement implies -almost states indeed in so many words (though a lawyer would find it a simple matter to read more or less into the thing than actually appears). But the men discovered upon the very first day that rain rendered outside work impracticable, that they received no pay for that day.
In fact, if they ceased work, say at four in the afternoon, owing to bad weather, they received only eight hours' pay. This, in effect, is hourly pay, and in direct disregard of the terms of the contract. However, after a meeting between the men and Mr. Pratt it was agreed that when the various foremen considered the weather too inclement for the men to remain out, the latter should receive a full day's pay. This, undoubtedly, was a concession-a step in the right direction-but it still remains-and this is the rock upon which the ship will ultimately split-that if the weather is too bad for the men to turn out at all in the morning they receive nothing. They are actually each in debt to the amount of seventy-five cents for their day's board. This is an undesirable condition of affairs. What the men ask for and what they certainly are entitled to, is straight time. Whether they will receive it or not is a question for the future to decide.
I desire especially to call the attention of the Minister of Railways to this phase of the matter. If these men have a substantial grievance, as the writer of this article represents, it is only right and fair that this grievance should be removed, and that the conditions of the men who are to carry on the work at Port Nelson in future be rendered as bearable as possible, and their wages paid to them without any deductions.
With reference to the tug Kathleen, which was the only tug, as I understand it, employed in the towing business at Port Nelson last season, I quote:
The purchase of a Halifax lobster tug by the Government for use at Port Nelson to pull massively heavy tows laden with the heaviest of construction material up Nelson river, eight miles, against a seven knot current, comes in for considerable ridicule. This chapter of mismanagement rivals all previous records In the story of Hudson bay.
The Kathleen's history on Halifax harbour showed her to be a nine knot craft, with a possible speed of eleven knots under pressure. When she tied up with an ordinary tow of lobster boats she could make two knots an hour. On the Nelson river, against the current of seven knots an hour, with a heavy tow, the Kathleen slipped back faster than she went ahead.
The Minister of Railways told the hon. member (Mr. A. K. Maclean) that the 44i
Kathleen was purchased from a gentleman in Halifax, who I believe is a political supporter of the Prime Minister. I do not desire to intimate for a moment that the political relationship existing between the owner of the Kathleen and the right hon. gentleman had anything to do with the purchase, but I do say that the Kathleen was utterly unfit, in respect to her machinery and towing power, for the service for which she was acquired. The inadequacy of the Kathleen was one of the reasons why so many thousand dollars worth of costly material was lost in the Hudson bay last year. The whole record of the expedition indicates that gross mismanagement characterized it from start to finish, and I believe that when the losses are figured up the total loss to the Dominion of Canada, resulting from this mismanagement, will be in the neighbourhood of $200,000. When the papers are brought down, I presume the information we seek will be contained in them.

When the papers are brought down, if there is any real discrepancy in the facts as given to the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) by those who were in Hudson bay last season, and the information possessed by the Department of Railways, the House will be in position to judge of the merits of the question.

With reference to the men who came back, I am only awaiting the report of Mr. McLaughlin, the engineer in charge down there, to arrive at a decision as to whether they should be paid or not. I have heard only one side of the question so far.

The hon. minister and the hon. memher for Brandon (Mr. Aikins) both stated that the conditions at the mouths of the rivers Mersey and Thames are similar to the conditions at the mouth of the Nelson river. Would these gentlemen state what the natural conditions are that bring about this similarity?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. gentlemen
have already spoken, and it is not permissible for them to speak again.

My information is that very powerful dredges have to be kept at work throughout the entire year to render navigation practicable at the mouths of the Mersey and Thames. That is particularly true of the Mersey because of the

shifting sand, and if there be a like condition at the mouth of the Nelson, it would go far to militate against the success of that port from a commercial point of view. I trust that the Minister of Railways, or the member for Brandon, will give us information on that point now or at some future time.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (South Renfrew): The argument of my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) has been well supported by hon. gentlemen who have taken part in this discussion, but what I want particularly to refer to is a remark of the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Aikins) criticising the action or non-action of the late Government. I can realize, that, desiring to make a speech to his constituents, and not having looked into the question, finding that the nearest thing at hand to hit was the late Government, he acted accordingly. This is a question which is too big to be discussed from a partisan standpoint. It has been in the public mind for over half a century.
How many years were you surveying before you started the work?
to that port. And that is not easy. I am not surprised that he rubs his brow when he gets up against this end of the scheme.
That belongs to another department.

The responsibility of
making the whole project successful, I am afraid, will be left mainly with the Railway Department-I believe it would have been had the former Government remained in power. If it is to be a success, you cannot relieve the Railway Department of responsibility, even though the building of the railway is the smallest part of the project Of course the Marine Department is responsible for buoying the channel No one department of the Government is responsible for this scheme; it is the Government in its entirety that is responsible. Under the late Government, the Marine Department, if I remember rightly, sent a steamer up to the Hudson bay and made a hydrographic survey. The Marine Department should have carried this work on up to the point at which the Railway Department could take hold of it and carry out the improvements, whichever harbour were chosen. Whatever censure should be placed upon any department in reference to the non-buoying of the channel, or the neglect to mark it out, should be placed upon the Marine Department, and I am sorry the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is not here to discuss that phase of the matter. Something was done by the late Government when they sent the steamships up to the straits of Hudson bay to make a hydrographic survey with a view to assisting in this great project. As to the harbour itself, as I pointed out a moment ago, the work is only half done-no, not half or nearly half done-when the railway reaches the seaboard on Hudson bay. What seaboard is the minister going to reach? It is no difficult thing to see which harbour is the best. There are no two ways of viewing the matter. Approaching it from the railway standpoint only, there is no doubt at all, but that Nelson has the better harbour. It affords the best terminal facilities, and, so far as the railway is concerned, saves 85 miles of hauling which would be involved in the case of the adoption of Fort Churchill as a terminal port. As I say, from a railway standpoint, there is no question as to which port is advisable; I am inclined to think that Nelson is the port anyway. I do not want to pose as an expert or authority in the matter; I base my opinion upon the reports I received from the various engineers.
tMr. Graham.]
The House will pardon me if I again go back to what the late Government did in the matter. We had a staff of engineers at Nelson and at Churchill during the whole of one winter, making observations and soundings. Their report to me was that there was a safe channel in the Nelson river, but that it would need some dredging to make it straight, to put it in ordinary terms. The Nelson river is not a small stream; it is a river into which flow the Saskatchewan, the Red river and other tributaries. It. is a large and comparatively swift-running stream; hon. gentlemen of the House must not get the idea that in discussing this river they are dealing with some small stream like the Nation river. The Nelson is a mighty river. I think the Ontario Government has secured a right of way in order that they may, if they so desire, build a railway up to the Nelson river; I imagine they consider that Nelson harbour will be a fairly good one. To make a comparison between Nelson and Churchill from the information given me by the engineers -and that is the only information upon which I base my opinion-Churchill at the present time is the better harbour for a limited amount of shipping accommodation. If a large business is to be done on this Hudson Bay route, Nelson is the harbour. In other words, Nelson is capable of being made into a harbour that will take care of any amount of traffic, while Churchill could not possibly be enlarged, except at enormous expense, to take care of any more traffic than it can take care of at the present time, which is comparatively small. If we expect the Hudson Bay route to be successful, it is worth while considering whether we should adopt the harbour that will eventually lend itself to development for increased trade. The engineers of the Railway Department pointed out to me the difficulties at Nelson, and they pointed out some of the advantages of Churchill; I have summed up very briefly the opinions I formed. For several miles out, Nelson harbour is practically the Nelson river. The channel of the harbour at the present time is undoubtedly crooked, but that there is a channel there I am convinced by soundings, the record of which I have in my possession, and which I looked for to-day but could not find. I am convinced that there is a channel from the Hudson bay right up into the Nelson river. The bed of the river is, I think, composed of what they call boulder clay, and it is capable of being bleared out and the channel straightened to a width of say 800 feet. The con-

dition to which the hon. member for Kings, P.E.I., (Mr. Hughes) referred may prevail; that is, the department may have to do periodical dredging on acount of the washing of sand down the river. That I am not prepared to say, but that the channel can be made at Nelson is quite evident, unless the engineers of the Railway Department were all wrong. Take, for instance, the entrance of one of the Empresses to Liverpool. They have a pretty narrow channel there, and it is subject to high seas, but no person would say that it is impracticable, as it is used all the time by the larger vessels. I am convinced that Nelson harbour can be made a magnificent harbour, tout the entrance to it will always be narrowed in proportion to the width of the Nelson river, which really gives us the harbour.. What will be the cost of the entire project; railway, elevators, docks, harbours, demarcation of channel by Marine Department, steamship line, and possibly elevators on the other side? It is a problem which, when you come to carry it out to its ultimate solution, may well demand the serious consideration of the House and the Government, and we should not dismiss it after but a few moments' discussion. Should the Government proceed to arrange at once for the construction of docks, having selected a port? Every one will say yes; they should at once proceed with the making of the harbour by clearing out the channel. If it is to be a harbour at all, that must be done. When that is done, and the elevators constructed, what are you going to do with the wheat or the merchandise coming in or going out? Will the shipowners come to Hudson bay of their own accord and enter into this traffic? I had discussions with some of them, and the different views they took upon this question were remarkable. Some large companies said to me: Yes, we will enter into this carrying trade if the Government will encourage us by cash subsidies. Others said: We will enter into this trade during part of the year, but we have to have specially constructed ships. I am not sure that the latter is the case. The bay itself is free from ice during many months of the year.
How many?

During a longer time than the harbour is at Montreal. The
bay itself is free from ice for months, but the difficulty with the navigation will be in the straits. There will be no difficulty unless on account, of the ice coming down the river into the bay. The late Governor General (pointed out that the Hudson bay is the Mediterranean of the north; he was surprised with the extent to which the bay was free from ice. But, as I say, the difficulty is in the strait. For two or three months in the year I do not believe specially constructed vessels will be necessary, but I may be wrong in that; vessel owners themselves seem to disagree on that point.
I am merely making these interrogations to impress on the minds of the Government-perhaps that is unnecessary-but on the minds of the country, the extreme necessity of proceeding at once if this is to be made a substantial aid to the solution of the transportation problem, in not only building the road, which is a small portion of the scheme but in completing the terminals finally and adequately, and looking out for some means of handling the traffic once it is established. I have tried to speak on this not in a controversial way.
I feel that somebody has made a bad blunder this year and the bad effect is not so much the loss of the money but the fact that to those who say that the road is impracticable this is a sweet morsel, and I have had a good many thumps from some of my friends, not in the West, in the last year, pointing out what a muddle I got the Government of Canada into inaugurating this Hudson Bay project. To those who are apposed to Nelson, whatever the object may be, this is also a sweet morsel, because they have pointed out to me in the last few months that if Churchill had been selected none of these calamities would have taken place. But the project is a good one and can overcome even the black eye of this year, and if the Government will proceed, I do not say rashly, to close up the gap and make arrangements suitable for the completion Df the project, arranging for the water end of the route as well as the land end, I believe we in this House will yet see the goods conveyed from the West to the mother country and from the mother country to the West, at a profit to all concerned and a special profit to the people of western Canada.
Motion agreed to.

For a copy of all letters, telegrams, and written resquests during the years 1912 and 1913, addressed to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, or the Naval or Marine branches of said department, or any officer or persons of either branch, by any person or persons,

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I would suggest to my hon. friend from Guysboro, who is acting for my hon. friend from Yarmouth (Mr. Law), a slight amendment. The motion reads:
Addressed to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, or the Naval or Marine Brari'ches of said department,
The Naval Department, of course, is a department just as much as the Department of Marine and Fisheries is, and it is evidently the Naval Depart-6 p.m. ment that is wanted here. I - would suggest that the motion be amended as follows:
Addressed to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, or the Department of Naval Affairs, or any officer of either department.
That would cover the information which I think the hon. member for Yarmouth is seeking.
Motion, as amended, agreed to.
I would like to know what is to be the business of the House to-morrow-whether it is to be a Government day or a private Members' day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I understand it is a
Government day, so the Clerk of the House informs me.

It all depends upon what we are to understand by the word ' week.' Rule 25 says that on Thursdays, after the expiration of the first four weeks, Government orders shall have precedence. The question is, when does that commence? It will be four weeks tomorrow since we met, and if you count Thursday as the first day on which the week is to commence, to-morrow will be the fourth week; but it seems to me hardly fair that the commencement of the week should be the day on which we first met. It ought to be the day following, Friday, and then we would have to-morrow as a private Members' day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think the four weeks
will be completed with the conclusion of this day's business. So far as the question

of Thursday is concerned, my right hon. friend will remember that it was his proposal to have Thursday as a Government day from the very beginning of the session, and that it was I who secured the four weeks for private members. I do not see that there is anything unfair in following the obvious intention of the rule. Heretofore the rule has not come into question, so far as I remember at the moment, because the fourth Thursday happened to come in the Christmas vacation. This is the first time the question has actually arisen. I understand the four weeks will terminate with to-day's business, and to-morrow we commence with the practice provided by the rule.
At six o'clock the House adjourned without question put, pursuant to rule.
Thursday, February 12, 1914.
